Context & sources

Explicit mode contract · FPS as your existing avatar

Put on your wash uniform. You are still you.

The intended minigame is first person. The player enters as their existing avatar, just as in the Hot Wheels game. The interactive canvas above is a surface-tool experiment, not yet the shared avatar/FPS runtime. It must not be mistaken for a replacement player controller.

01

Choose the mission

Approach the carwash as your avatar. Accept the invitation or keep exploring. The shared game transition parks the entering vehicle and preserves the player, outfit, loadout and world return point.

02

Uniform first

The first mission step puts a fun carwash uniform on the same avatar: an apron, boots and gloves. Use the shared wardrobe system for this temporary outfit. Your identity and underlying character never change.

03

Work, then return

Use the shared FPS controls at the wash station. Finish with a partial score, pause, or leave through the standard game exit. Restore the previous control mode and outfit, and return to the same world with the same vehicle.

One player. Shared systems.

The minigame owns wash progress, tool state, score and mission objectives. The game owns player identity, avatar, input, camera modes, wardrobe, inventory, pause and scene transitions. The wash requests these services through their existing integration points; it must never replace their owners or install a competing controller. Missing assets may use low-poly placeholders while keeping this FPS contract explicit.

Controls must agree with the mode

Movement, look, interaction, pointer capture, touch controls and pause/exit follow the shared FPS system. While operating the machine, surface strokes take priority over camera look through the shared interaction-mode arbitration. Opening a menu releases tool contact. Part selection moves the wash turntable/work view in 0.25 seconds; the three zoom levels are station views, not another player or free-flight controller. Resume, cancel and exit restore controls predictably.

Applies beyond this wash

Hot Wheels and other avatar-played minigames declare their mode before entry and use the same lifecycle. Joining a thief pursuit suspends the wash mission through the shared transition system. It does not create a new player, lose the uniform/vehicle relationship, or overwrite the world state. Avatar/FPS integration, dressing and transitions are explicit acceptance requirements, not features implemented in this canvas.

The question for this round

Does washing with a giant robot feel like painting with your finger?

The car is the canvas. The wash bay is a cheerful Overland workshop: mint-painted machinery, coral joints, big brushes, enamel tiles, warm timber and green hills outside. Your cursor is the tool tip. The machine bends to meet it immediately. A dirty wheel becomes a little project; a huge sweep across the bonnet becomes a glorious reveal.

Evan’s direction, preserved

“The apparatus was articulating robotic doers that were immediately responsive and acted like brushes to your cursor.” Every run starts with a super-filthy car. Maximize score by literally washing its different parts. Earn decoration packs for whichever vehicle went through.

01

Arrive outrageously dirty

Your own car rolls into the bay under a fresh coat of baked mud, wheel sludge and bird splats. A replay always creates a complete new mess. You never need to drive around gathering dirt first.

02

Conduct the machines

Spray foam, scrub panels, burrow into wheels, rinse, then buff. One active arm tracks your finger; other arms wait in their docks. Switch tools without an animation lock. Turn the car to reach the far side.

03

Make the reveal count

Every rinse, scrub, wax and dry action adds to your score. Even a partial wash advances this vehicle’s decoration pack. Unwrap it, try it on, then return to the world.

A busy wash. A simple job.

Explore a giant soft sponge, a precise tire-pressure nozzle, a foam cannon and a waxing mitt. Rollers spin, hoses flex and water splashes around the bay. The robot’s elbow can bounce; the contact point must not lag. Comedic splashes must never hide the patch you are aiming at.

ToolYour handThe car
Foam cannonSweep a broad fanMud softens; no points for repeatedly foaming the same patch.
Big scrubberScribble circles or long strokesBody grime breaks away along your stroke. Pre-soaked areas clear faster.
Tire pressure jetTrace the tire and rimSludge peels away under a concentrated water jet.
Rinse jetChase the sudsFoam washes away, exposing clean paint. Stubborn dirt needs another scrub.
Waxing mittSweep clean, rinsed panelsBuild a glossy finish, earning credit for each new waxed area.
DryerSweep warm air over the carDroplets disappear; each newly dry area earns credit.

Every part within reach

Tap a part on the little car map: front, rear, top, left side, right side or tires. The turntable and camera settle into that view in 0.25 seconds. Three zoom levels—Whole, Part and Close—keep navigation predictable. The rotation slider remains available for in-between angles. Tool contact pauses during a view change so a camera move cannot accidentally scrub.

A score for every bit of work

Rinse → soap → scrub the top and sides → pressure-wash the tires → rinse → wax → dry. There is plenty happening inside the carwash, but the job stays simple. No timer, frantic combos or failure pressure. Finish whenever you like and receive a score for the work you actually did.

This experiment: rinse and soap prepare each body patch; scrubbing removes dirt; the tire jet quickly clears tire sludge. Rinse away the suds, wax the clean surface, and blow it dry. Each patch has a finite point budget. Partial progress counts, and repeating a completed action cannot farm points. Ten thousand points represents a fully completed wash, not a required pass mark.

The same cars. Two ways to earn the cruiser.

Latest intake from Evan: use the same cars that are available at the skate park. Their stable identity, colors and decorations travel between activities. Completing either the carwash mission or the skate-park mission unlocks the cruiser in driving mode. This is one shared unlock owned by the host game, not two independently spawned cruisers.

Art direction: Epic Hero-quality source models, likely through STL / Meshy workflows, with lower-poly, lo-fi representations in the running game. Preserve the appealing silhouettes and proportions. The current buggy and toy-car builders remain study placeholders; they do not establish the final shared roster.

Still to decide: what counts as mission completion for the cruiser unlock. The research chat proposed that finishing even a partial wash could qualify; Evan has not yet specified that threshold. Partial-work points remain guaranteed, but a partial score and the cruiser completion condition are separate decisions. Completing the second mission must not duplicate the shared unlock; its own cosmetic reward is a proposal.

Proposed synthesis from the reference chat — for exploration

Working title: Cruiser Cleanup. A familiar, filthy car gets a celebratory reveal. Consider selectable soap colors, colorful soap tanks, a drain, organized tool docks and a decoration display. A current-treatment ring could complement overall cleanliness; Cleanliness, Shine and Care are suggested score categories, not approved rules. The existing simple, untimed washing loop and same-avatar FPS contract take precedence.

Possible small surprises: muddy puppy pawprints, rainbow bubbles or a wandering duck. These are alternatives to explore, not a cancellation of the requested optional thief/chase/call-for-help story. A “Drive your cruiser” reveal is proposed after the host confirms the shared unlock.

These are integration requirements and proposals; this Level 1 canvas does not write cruiser unlocks or garage inventory.

A prize for this car

All partial-wash scores advance a decoration pack for the vehicle in the bay. The first example, Bubble Parade, adds a pink accent; a developed pack could include bubble decals, wheel trims and antenna ornaments. Later packs could explore Meadow Picnic and Disco Sparkle. In this study, 1,500 accumulated points unlock the example color preview for that vehicle. Scores and rewards last only for this browser session; they do not write to the game garage. Threshold and pack contents are exploration choices.

What is real in this exploration?

Real repo vehicle geometry, turntable, surface hit-testing, articulated tool motion, per-patch rinse/soap/dirt/wax/dry state, score, fresh filthy runs, two vehicles and a session-only reward preview. The Moon buggy uses the game builder; the toy car is the repo’s existing placeholder. Grime and workshop machinery are study geometry. Fine dirt masks, crevice cleaning, final animation, scoring balance, music synchronization and saved rewards remain later work.

Borrow the feeling. Build our own wash.

Crayola Scribble Scrubbie

Evan confirmed this reference with a gameplay screenshot. We observed its centered creature, colorful wash room, turntable and distinct tools. The official app describes 3D coloring and a Pet Washing Station. We take direct touch, visible surface change and affection for the object. Robot tools, partial-work scores and vehicle rewards are our additions. Official app listing · Crayola wash-and-recolor toy.

Evan’s local Game Oracle

Queried locally for washing, PowerWash, Scribble, Overcooked and arcade. No cleaning/Scribble matches were present. Overcooked! 2 supplied source-reported colorful 3D, overhead presentation and animated props. Our inference: keep cheerful chaos readable around one clear task. The director was consulted again after Evan clarified that the machinery is visually busy but the task is simple. It returned source: studies, model: null; a generic retrieval template, not an expert model endorsement. Consultation record.

Earlier carwash direction

The prior study proposed a four-minute conveyor and musical stations. We retain its cheerful wash identity and customization, but replace passive travel with direct surface work. Mandatory song timing and the buggy-only prize are superseded. Preserved tunnel study.

Provenance

Rules here are our synthesis of Evan’s brief, Oracle records and Crayola’s descriptions. We did not play or reverse-engineer Crayola’s app. No Crayola art, code, characters or audio is used. See the Context card for project sources.

And sometimes, a story interrupts.

The wash is simple; the world can still surprise you. Evan’s example: a thief tries to rob the carwash. An optional invitation lets you call the police and chase after them. Keep washing is a real choice, too. If you join, park the wash state exactly as it is—vehicle, dirt, soap, wax, score and tool—and resume it when you return.

Exploration, not implemented here: a playful pursuit with a clear destination, a call-for-help action, and a return to the bay. No lost cleaning progress, forced chase or repeated interruption. We still need to explore frequency, chase controls and the resolution. The key-frame research verified a suspicious/non-paying customer event in Express Car Wash Simulator | Demo, including an escape sequence around 25:48–26:08. It did not verify a police call or a robbery of the premises. Our call-for-help pursuit remains Evan’s proposed addition. View the 11 timestamped reference frames and gameplay breakdown.

The world invites. The player chooses.

Approaching an event in player mode should offer Play or Keep exploring. Proximity or hovering highlights the event but never starts its mission or steals steering. For overlapping events, the targeted nearby event wins. Walking away dismisses the invitation; returning makes it available again.

Vehicle continuity

Capture the entering vehicle’s stable ID and loadout. Wash that exact vehicle, grant compatible decorations to it, then restore it at the exit. No silent switch to a Moon buggy.

Broken model

The supplied screenshot shows pale repeated geometry obscuring the vehicle. Investigate silhouette/occlusion passes, materials and transforms before altering the asset. This study does not claim a driving-model fix.

Reversed steering

Verify keyboard and touch left/right in the chase camera, forward and reverse. The driver’s +Z convention needs a view-relative regression test. This study does not change driving physics.

Next exploration

Review tool immediacy, vehicle readability and clean trails. Then refine pressure, brush sizes, top/side access, wax and drying feedback, and decoration-pack unboxing. Study publication, finished game quality and live integration are separate milestones.
